items.title: Show HN: Tessary – Find the AI agent failures your sampled evals miss
items.summary: Hey, I'm Akhil, co-founder of Tessary. An open-source agent reliability platform that monitors every production trace, detects issues that sampled evals miss, and investigates to find the root cause. We started up about a year ago building synthetic users for usability testing of B2B software, we built the agents that would personify real users and use the software but, we were never able to make them work reliably enough for long running sessions. We had built a massive eval set to tune our agents but, then the evaluation itself got prohibitively costly - like 5x costlier than actually running the agent since we needed to grade across the many narrow intents of our agent. That's where Tessary originated, we wanted to make agent reliability both cover more ground and be simultaneously less costly to run. Tessary works on 2 layers. L1 classifiers - which look at every agent trace and flag potentially erroneous ones extremely cheaply. We are talking 2-3 orders of magnitude cheaper than running the actual agent. L2 agents - which triage and find the root cause of the issue from the erroneous traces. These are run on SOTA models but, because we run them on already flagged traces, the time and $ spent finding the cause is much cheaper than running grading on even 1% of traces. In our testing on complex agents, at 1M traces, this approach was 5x cheaper than sampled evaluations and as your agent gets more reliable, the cost of reliability also goes down. we are open source and can be self-hosted so, you don't need to send your traces to us. We support existing `gen_ai` spec and ingestion over OTLP so, you can add this as a new exporter to your existing setup. We have a cloud version, you can quickly try the features with a $10 credit. We are looking to build more classifiers and enable people to build custom classifiers for their needs and would love to hear feedback on common failure modes people have built solutions or evaluation for Repo: https://github.com/tessaryai/tessary Website: https://tessary.ai Try for free: https://app.tessary.ai

Show HN: SqlFlow – Durable Workflows Backed by PostgreSQL or SQL Server
items.summary: Hey HN! I have built SqlFlow, which is an open-source durable workflow engine backed by PostgreSQL or SQL Server, with SDKs for .NET, Java, Python, and Go. Workflows support retries, checkpoints, rate limitng, scheduling, and suspension while waiting for events. It took a large deal of inspiration from Absurd, but it expands on the core concepts. Instead of polling the database, it supports native database features such as PostgreSQL LISTEN / NOTIFY, SQL Server Service Broke, and you could also use NATS. The durable state always remains in your SQL database. Each SDK comes with a complete example, that models an AI Agent Workflow: - https://github.com/bytefish/SqlFlow/tree/main/sdks I would love to hear your feedback.

Show HN: PodcastDelay – an open source RSS feed generator
items.summary: I'm a bit nostalgic. There are some podcasts I started listening to years ago (2017~), but not at the start (2008~). At a certain point, the podcast changes, maybe some stalwarts rotate out of the main line-up... I just want to go back, to the beginning. I'm also someone that has no self-restraint. I'll mainline ten of the same podcast in a day, then forget all about listening to no.11. Podcasts apps do not help this: It's hard to get them to cooperate in a way which surfaces your next episode in the 'Latest episodes' list, because while it may be up next for you, it was actually released 15 years ago. PodcastDelay solves that, by taking that original feed and 'delaying' it by however long you want. It's a solution for re-publishing a podcast's RSS feed as a new private feed. It can start releasing from any episode, at any cadence, including mirroring the original release cadence. If a show has two feeds — the regular one and a premium/bonus one — you can merge them into a single delayed feed. Each bonus episode comes out the same distance after its free counterpart as it did originally: an hour stays an hour, a day stays a day, whatever cadence you're replaying the free feed at. Audio isn't hosted/reposted, but there are plenty of solutions if you wanted to have 'local' media turned into an RSS feed, which PodcastDelay could then put out in the correct cadence.

items.title: Show HN: Talus, a small terrain diffusion model that runs in the browser
items.summary: Talus is a small diffusion model that makes game heightmaps and runs entirely in the browser. try it at: https://talus.tersa.tech It has 23M parameters and it was trained from scratch. The training data was 45K maps from my own generator. I made it to get terrain I can ask for whenever. The best part is that it can run on a consumer GPU (For e.g. I trained it on an RTX 5060). It's limits are the 64x64 maps, and it was only trained on procedural maps. The GitHub link is: https://github.com/osfv/talus It's fully open source with the Apache License! items.title: Show HN: Lacuna – open-source inline AI writing suggestions for your Mac
items.summary: This past week I built (prompted) a tool I find myself using day to day and wanted to share it with others who may find it useful as well. “Lacuna” is an opinionated way to invoke LLMs into any text input on your Mac. Specifically, you can type bracketed phrases {such as this}, press Shift-Command-K (or a different shortcut of your choosing), and the tool sends your bracketed phrase + the surrounding text contents to an LLM of your configuration for generating text to replace the bracketed phrase. The program returns 3 candidate phrases and the experience is entirely keyboard navigable. Demo: https://jackdamon.org/assets/images/lacuna-scheduling-demo.g... Example scheduling workflow using Lacuna’s native UI and sample suggestions. So far I find myself frequently using it when drafting emails where I want help with quick phrasing. The project was inspired by Rectangle, an open source utility app for window tiling that is keyboard based. Lacuna is open source and available here: https://github.com/jdamon96/lacuna Blog: https://jackdamon.org/blog/lacuna/
